title: De quibusdam eximiis proprietatibus circa divisores potestatum occurrentibus

deep.reconstruction: Context: E557 develops Euler's empirical approach to quadratic reciprocity. Theorem 4 (§16) says: if P = 4n-1 is prime, every number p = n + q^2 + q is a quadratic residue mod P. Euler deduces this from his earlier claim that p is a residue whenever 4p - (2q+1)^2 is prime. A direct check makes it trivial: 4n ≡ 1 (mod P), so n ≡ 1/4 and p ≡ q^2 + q + 1/4 = (q + 1/2)^2 (mod P). The scholion §19 then raises the deeper conjecture that every prime factor of every such p is also a residue mod P. This page tests that conjecture numerically. For P = 3, 7, 11, 19, 23, 31, 43, 47, 59, 67, 71, 79, 83 (n = 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 11, 12, 15, 17, 18, 20, 21), Euler lists, factored, the first 9-12 values of p = n + q + q^2 (q = 0, 1, 2, ...). He then lists the primes r occurring in them; each r is a quadratic residue mod P. In modern terms: 4p = (2q+1)^2 + P. Hence every odd prime l dividing p, other than P, satisfies (-P/l) = 1. Because P ≡ 3 (mod 4), quadratic reciprocity converts this to (l/P) = 1; for l = 2 the supplementary law gives the same. The conjecture is therefore exactly the reciprocity law for primes P ≡ 3 (mod 4), stated through the values of the principal form of discriminant -P. The tables for P = 43 and 67 (n = 11, 17) are wholly prime, the Euler/Rabinowitsch prime-producing polynomials for the Heegner discriminants. Euler makes no comment on this here; §20 on the next page discusses which small primes can enter the sequence.
errors: No arithmetic errors found. All p-values were checked against n+q+q^2, and all listed r against the quadratic residues mod 4n-1.
Minor convention: Euler includes the modulus P itself in the r-lists when it divides some p (3 in case 1, 7 in case 2, 11 in case 3, 19 in case 4), although P ≡ 0 is not properly a residue.

Euler's route to Theorem 4 (via the earlier unproved claim about 4p-(2q+1)^2 prime) is roundabout: the statement is trivially true because p ≡ (q+1/2)^2 mod P. The genuinely open part, the prime-factor claim, is equivalent to reciprocity and is left conjectural.

deep.surprise_reason: These are correct numerical tables supporting a known Euler formulation of reciprocity, which historians have already covered. The class-number-one examples (43, 67) appear implicitly, but Euler's prime-generating trinomials are well known.
transcription_corrections: Transcription agrees with the image. In case 1 the p-list correctly reads 1, 3, 7, 13, 3·7, 31, 43, 3·19, 73, 7·13, 3·37. In case 1° the scan shows the p-list after the r-list; the transcription reverses the order.
